paras: The threats against Mormon missionaries in Union County, Tennessee, were threats of lynching reported in February 1882 against Mormon missionaries who had won converts, some of them Black, in Union County in East Tennessee. No violence was reported, and the episode is known only from a short Chattanooga dispatch and Tennessee rewrites of it.

According to a Chattanooga dispatch dated February 8, Mormon missionaries were "hard at work" in Union County and had "secured a number of converts, notably some negros." Tennessee papers described the missionaries as active in "Union and other counties in East Tennessee," with converts "notably among the negroes."

The wire report said that communities were "wrought up against them and threats of lynching are made," without saying who was threatened. The Clarksville Weekly Chronicle, which prefaced the item with "It is said," and later the Memphis Daily Appeal made the target explicit: the threat was of "lynching them if they do not leave," meaning the missionaries. None of the reports names the missionaries, gives their race or number, names a town, or identifies anyone who made the threats.
No report of an attack, arrest or departure of the missionaries appears in the coverage.

The National Associated Press item ran on February 9 in Western dailies, including the Omaha Daily Bee under "Mormon Converts," the Salt Lake Herald, the Cheyenne Daily Leader, the Sacramento Daily Record-Union and the Eureka Daily Sentinel, which headed it "Opposed to the Mormons." In Tennessee it appeared without comment in state-news columns, in Clarksville on February 11 and in Memphis on February 15.

Condensed briefs in the Daily Kennebec Journal, the River Falls Journal, the Canton Advocate and the Rocky Mountain Husbandman kept the Black converts but dropped the threats. A Sedalia Eagle editorial reprinted in the Kirksville Weekly Graphic took up the converts rather than the threats, saying that "the negroes of the South are falling victims" to Mormonism and joking about "white and black wives" in Utah. No paper in the coverage commented on the lynching threats themselves.
